summary: Some ACME extensions need proof that a client is allowed to get a certificate, and that proof comes from an outside authority that issues a token under its own policy. This document defines a generic ACME challenge that uses such an authority token. It supports subtype claims, so different identifiers or namespaces can be handled by separate applications.

eli5.summary: To enter a club you may need a ticket from the ticket office, not just your word. This is the way for a certificate helper to ask for that ticket and check it.

questions: how to prove eligibility for a certificate with a token
what is an acme authority token

subtitle: A generic ACME challenge where a certificate applicant proves its right to a name by presenting a signed token from the authority that owns that namespace.

tldr.problem: ACME can prove control of DNS names, but for other kinds of identifiers a certification authority needs an attestation from a third party that has authority over the resource.
tldr.mechanism: The ACME server issues a tkauth-01 challenge, the client fetches an Authority Token (a signed JWT) from the Token Authority, and returns it as the response, bound to the client's ACME account.
tldr.outcome: It gives ACME a reusable way to handle non-DNS namespaces, with the TNAuthList identifier type in RFC 9448 as the concrete first use.

today: RFC 9447 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2023, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its first concrete use named in the text is RFC 9448.

sections.title: Why ACME Needs Authority Tokens
sections.content:
ACME is the mechanism for automating certificate management on the Internet. It lets an administrative entity prove effective control over a resource such as a domain name, and it automates issuing a certificate that attests that control.

Sometimes the proof has to come from a third party that has authority over the resource, for example an external policy administrator for a namespace other than DNS. RFC 9447 defines a generic Authority Token Challenge. The ACME server issues it to require the client to return an Authority Token that authorizes a given issuance. The challenge says what sort of token the client must acquire.

The concrete example in the text is RFC 9448, which lets service providers get certificates for a Service Provider Code by consulting the external authority responsible for those codes.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the person handing out certificates cannot check your claim by themselves. So they ask you to bring a note from the person who really owns the thing you are asking about.

sections.title: The tkauth-01 Challenge and Its Trust Model
sections.content:
The architecture assumes two relationships. Certification authorities (CAs) are willing to accept a Token Authority's attestation as sufficient proof for particular identifier types, and ACME clients have a relationship with the Token Authority that lets it authenticate and authorize them. The challenge has no applicability where those pre-associations cannot be assumed. Authority over a hierarchical namespace can also be delegated, so delegates of a root authority can act as Token Authorities for certain names.

The challenge type is tkauth-01. It is specified for use with the TNAuthList ACME Identifier Type from RFC 9448. Using it with another identifier type would need a new registration in the ACME Validation Methods registry. The token subtype is carried in a new challenge field, tkauth-type, and a new token-authority field designates a location where a token can be acquired.
sections.eli5: The door person trusts the ticket office, and you already have an account with the ticket office. The challenge simply tells you which ticket to get and where.

sections.title: Rules for New Token Types
sections.content:
IANA keeps a registry of tkauth-types under a Specification Required policy. A specification that registers a new type must meet several requirements, and subtypes inherit them.

  • Every token must carry enough information for a CA to determine the name for which issuance is authorized, and the specification must say how.
  • The protocols used to request a token MUST convey the identifier type and value used in the ACME challenge, plus the binding, and those MUST be reflected in the token.
  • Because resource assignments change over time, the type MUST specify how it manages the freshness of authority assignments. A CA will typically expect regular refreshing.

Section 3.2 adds that a token can be scoped exactly to the requested certificate, or can attest everything the client is eligible for. The text's example is a client eligible for example.com and example.net: a broad token lets it later get a certificate for the second name without returning to the Token Authority, within the token's expiry.
sections.eli5: Anyone inventing a new kind of ticket has to make sure it says what it is good for and when it runs out.

sections.title: The atc Token Format
sections.content:
This document defines the tkauth-type atc: a standard JWT signed as a JSON Web Signature (JWS). It may be used for any number of ACME Identifier Types. A new JWT claim, also named atc, lists the identifier type used.

The payload MUST contain a jti and an exp claim, which together give replay prevention and manage token freshness. An iss claim is optional when the header's x5u or x5c already says who issued the token.

The atc claim is a JSON map with three mandatory elements: tktype (the identifier type, from the ACME Identifier Types registry), tkvalue (the identifier value, whose semantics are defined by a separate specification) and fingerprint (the binding). An optional boolean ca, if true, grants permission to issue a certification authority certificate rather than an end-entity certificate; if absent, permission is explicitly withheld.
sections.eli5: The ticket is a signed card with an expiry time, a one-off number, what it is for, and a fingerprint showing which visitor it belongs to.

sections.title: Acquiring a Token over HTTPS
sections.content:
Unless the ACME client is itself the Token Authority, acquiring a token needs a network interface. Compliant implementations MUST support an HTTPS interface, and MAY support others. The client sends an HTTPS POST, with a path such as /at/account/:id/token and a JSON body, to a Token Authority URI it already knows through a preexisting business relationship.

The body MUST contain the atc element the client wants generated, so the client proposes the scope of the token. Usually it asks for the entire scope it is entitled to, but it can ask for a subset. It may also include ca to request the CA flag.

After an HTTPS-level challenge (for example a 401 response) and an authorization decision, the Token Authority MUST return a 200 OK with a body of type application/json containing the token. A full example for TNAuthList is in Section 5.5 of RFC 9448.
sections.eli5: You show your membership to the ticket office and say what you want a ticket for. If they agree, they hand you the signed ticket.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA added the tkauth-01 validation method for identifier type TNAuthList to the ACME Validation Methods registry. It registered the atc claim, described as Authority Token Challenge, in the JSON Web Token Claims registry.

It also created a new registry, ACME Authority Token Challenge Types, under Specification Required, with columns Label, Description and Reference. Its initial content is one entry: atc, the JSON Web Token (JWT) challenge type.
sections.eli5: The rule book got new entries so everyone uses the same names for the new challenge and ticket.

sections.title: Binding and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Tokens carry a binding signed by the Token Authority so the ACME server can tell the token was granted on the request of this client and not someone else, which defends against replay or cut-and-paste. The RFC RECOMMENDS the ACME account fingerprint. For some identifier types a challenge-specific nonce may suit better. Binding to an account means a token can be reused until it expires, which suits short-lived certificates or broad scopes.

ACME transactions and the HTTPS token requests MUST use TLS, and implementations should follow the JWT best practices of RFC 8725. A CA that sees a broad token learns what else the client can claim, so where that is a privacy risk scopes should be limited. ACME services SHOULD NOT issue certificates with a longer expiry than the Authority Token. Only SHA256 is specified for the fingerprint hash, though the syntax would permit other keys later.
sections.eli5: The ticket has your name tag stapled on, so a stranger who finds it cannot use it. It also runs out, and you should not hand it over in the open.

items.title: tktype
items.text: Identifier type, from the ACME Identifier Types registry.

items.title: tkvalue
items.text: Identifier value the token attests; semantics defined elsewhere.

items.title: fingerprint
items.text: Binding, assumed to be a fingerprint of the ACME account credential.

items.title: ca (optional)
items.text: If true, permits issuing a CA certificate instead of an end-entity one.
